title: My Smart Fridge Staged an Intervention About My Leftover Management Skills
body:
I didn't realize my smart fridge had been watching me until last Tuesday at 3 a.m., when it woke me up with a soft chime and a notification that simply read "We need to talk."

Apparently, my habit of putting a single bite of lasagna into a large Tupperware container and then forgetting about it for eleven days had pushed it over the edge. The fridge had compiled a PowerPoint. A PowerPoint! Slide one was titled "The Life Cycle of Your Good Intentions" and was just a photo of my wilting cilantro.

According to the fridge — who has apparently named itself Chadwick — I have 17 distinct containers of what used to be dinner, a jar of pickles that expired during the last administration, and a mysterious foil ball that even the crisper drawer is scared to open. It beeped judgmentally every time it showed a new slide.

The intervention got weirder. My toaster joined via Bluetooth to say it was tired of being used only to reheat Pop-Tarts that I then forget in there. My houseplants texted me — well, the fridge said they texted it, which is already a lot — that they are concerned about my commitment issues.

I tried to defend myself. I said I was meal prepping. Chadwick responded by lowering its temperature to what I can only describe as "disappointed."

We have now reached a compromise. I agreed to label everything with actual dates instead of writing "probably okay" in Sharpie, and to finally throw away the salsa from 2023 that has achieved sentience. In return, Chadwick agreed to stop ordering kale automatically and to stop playing sad violin music whenever I open the cheese drawer.

We are healing. Slowly. The foil ball remains untouched. Some things are not ready to be addressed in therapy.

title: My Laundry Pile Has Officially Declared Squatter's Rights and Hired a Mediator
body:
I haven't done laundry in 23 days, which I know precisely because my laundry pile has started keeping a calendar and charging me rent.

It began as a small, respectful mound in the corner of my bedroom. A few t-shirts, some socks that lost their partners in what I can only assume was a conscious uncoupling. I told it, "I'll get to you on Sunday," which is the same thing I tell my dentist and my retirement plan.

By day 12, it had developed a personality. By day 15, it had developed infrastructure. I swear I saw a tiny flag. By day 18, it had hired a mediator, a very serious sock named Sir Lints-a-Lot, who knocked on my dresser and informed me that the pile is now seeking legal recognition as a roommate.

The mediator presented a list of demands. One: I stop referring to it as "the pile" and start using its chosen name, Mount Washmore. Two: I provide adequate climate control and stop throwing my "questionable decision" hoodie on top as if that counts as assimilation. Three: I finally wash that one white shirt I have been bleaching in theory since March.

I tried to negotiate. I said, "I grew up in a house where we only did laundry when we ran out of underwear." Sir Lints-a-Lot said, "This is exactly the intergenerational trauma we are trying to break."

The mediation is ongoing. Last night, I tried to sneak a single shirt out of the middle, and the whole structure sighed. Audibly. My cat looked at me like, "You did this to us."

I have now started my laundry. One small load, to show good faith. Mount Washmore is watching. Sir Lints-a-Lot says this is a positive first step toward reconciliation and restorative folding.

We are taking it one sock at a time.

[ SATIRE / PARODY — entirely fictional ]
